solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Don and Charlie redirected Aussie runner

parts.note: a charlie is British slang for a fool, as is an ass

indicators.note: sent back the other way, so the bird's name is read backwards

parts.note: the emu is a large flightless Australian bird that runs fast

explanation.surface: A man called Don and his friend Charlie steer an Australian athlete onto a new course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a name but is the verb meaning put on, and Charlie is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To don clothes is to put them on, and to take on a garment or role is another sense of the word.

clue.text: Scottish town admits Conservative extremists in the place

indicators.note: a place that admits someone lets them inside

parts.note: Alloa is a town in central Scotland

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its outer letters

explanation.surface: A Scottish town lets Conservative hardliners into the place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremists' here are just the first and last letters of 'the', TE.
explanation.definitionFit: To allocate is to assign or allot something to a position, so to place it.

clue.text: Carling, say, in a small group showing muscles

definitions.text: Carling, say, in a small group
definitions.meaning: Carling is a popular British lager, sold in packs of half a dozen cans
well-defined stomach muscles, slang for a toned abdomen

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a pack of six beer cans and also a set of visible abdominal muscles.

clue.text: Author's character I want to be cast

parts.note: a mark is a written character or sign

indicators.note: cast here means thrown into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A novelist says a particular character is what they want to be cast as.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' is a written sign, not a role; 'to be cast' shuffles I WANT into TWAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The American writer of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn wrote under this pen name.

clue.text: Start to suffer in the chest when dropping round, appearing ghostly

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only the beginning of suffer is used
dropping something means letting it go, so the round letter leaves the chest word

parts.note: pectoral means relating to the chest
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: A patient's first pains in the chest, after a fall, leave them looking pale as a ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the' and 'appearing' are link words; 'dropping' looks like a fall but removes the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectral describes something like a spectre, a phantom or apparition, so it is a synonym for ghostly.

clue.text: Former US musician Tom joins artist, old member of The Police

parts.note: Tom Petty was an American rock musician who died in 2017
John Constable was an English landscape painter

explanation.surface: A late American rock star teams up with a painter who once played in the band The Police.
explanation.walkthrough: The Police is the band, but here it means the actual force; a petty constable was an old parish law officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A petty constable was a historical local parish officer keeping the peace, so a former policeman.

clue.text: Yes-man's language quiet

parts.note: Cree is a language of a Native American people of Canada
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A sycophant's way of talking is soft and muted.
explanation.definitionFit: A creep is a toady who flatters superiors, the same fawning type as a yes-man.

clue.text: Soldier, and little woman with reserve, celebrate

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps, so a soldier
Jo is one of the sisters in the novel Little Women
ice means coolness or reserve of manner

explanation.surface: A soldier and his small, reserved wife have a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little woman' points to Jo March of Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: To rejoice is to show great joy, so to celebrate.

clue.text: Makes redundant from brick-building firm outside Teesside, in post

indicators.note: outside says the firm's name wraps around the postcode

parts.note: Lego is the Danish maker of plastic toy bricks
TS is the postcode area for Teesside in north-east England

explanation.surface: A building firm with a post on Teesside lays off staff.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'brick-building firm' is the Danish toy-maker, not a builder, and 'post' points to a postcode.
explanation.definitionFit: When an employer lets staff go it dismisses them, which is making them redundant.

clue.text: Titled brat Theo, having rampaged, summoned into court

parts.note: a person titled something is called that

indicators.note: rampaging means running wild, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A spoiled aristocratic child named Theo runs riot and gets a summons to court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having rampaged' shuffles BRAT THEO into TO THE BAR; the summons is to qualify as a barrister, not to stand trial.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone admitted as a barrister is formally invited to practise as an advocate before the courts.

clue.text: Long shift female ignored, working in a rut

indicators.note: something ignored is left out, so the female letter is dropped

parts.note: flux is a state of constant change or shifting

indicators.note: working suggests the letters are set in motion and rearranged

explanation.surface: A worker stuck in a rut does a long shift with the women left out of the rota.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' is the definition, as luxuriant hair grows long and thick; 'working' makes URIANT from IN A RUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Luxuriant growth, such as hair or foliage, is thick, abundant and flowing, which a crossword setter can stretch to long.

clue.text: Buffoon that I jeered somewhat when retreating

indicators.note: when retreating says the hidden letters are read backwards
somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone admits to having jeered at a clown who then backed away.
explanation.definitionFit: An eejit is Irish and Scottish slang for an idiot, a fool or buffoon.

clue.text: Near the main street, American's put in fuel

indicators.note: put in says these letters are placed inside the fuel word

parts.note: coal is a fuel burned for heat

explanation.surface: An American has put fuel into a car near the main street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the main' is the sea, not the main street; the inserted letters go after the second letter of the fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The main' is a literary term for the open sea, so places beside the sea are near the main.

clue.text: Typical behaviour of boxer, for instance to cough up over by ring

definitions.text: Typical behaviour of boxer, for instance

indicators.note: turned over means read backwards here

parts.note: cough up is slang for hand over money, to pay
a ping is a ringing sound, like a bell

explanation.surface: A boxer is told to cough up a fee for the ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxer is the dog breed, not a fighter; 'by' simply means next to.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogs such as boxers bark sharply and noisily, which is described as yapping.

clue.text: Hard wood, a rumoured item on Asian takeaway menu?

indicators.note: a rumour is passed on by word of mouth, so the words are heard rather than written

parts.note: teak is a hard wood, followed by a as written

explanation.surface: Talk of a hardwood item supposedly turning up on an Indian takeaway menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rumoured' says TEAK plus A is said aloud, giving a sound like the dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken tikka is a familiar dish of spiced marinated meat on Indian restaurant menus in Britain.

clue.text: Maybe dog's cross — repelled postman often seen here

indicators.note: driven back, so the combined letters are read in reverse

parts.note: a dog is an example of a pet, and the s comes from the apostrophe s
a rood is a cross or crucifix, especially in a church

explanation.surface: An angry dog fends off the postman who arrives most mornings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repelled' reverses PETS ROOD; the dog chasing postmen is the joke, but the dog is only a pet in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The postman delivers letters at the front door, so the step outside it is where he is regularly seen.

clue.text: Sun erred unfortunately — editor's last to resign

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone awry, so these letters are jumbled
last points to the final letter of the editor word

explanation.surface: A newspaper made a mistake and its editor finally has to quit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper; 'unfortunately' shuffles SUN ERRED.
explanation.definitionFit: To surrender is to give up or yield, which is what resigning means.

clue.text: Releases placed on Spotify primarily at no cost

parts.note: to set something is to place it

indicators.note: primarily means first, so only the opening letter of the streaming service is used

parts.note: free means costing nothing

explanation.surface: Songs are put on Spotify mainly at no charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Releases' looks like a noun for new music but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To liberate someone or let them go is to release them, so these are synonyms.

clue.text: A T. Rex perhaps touching small leaves

parts.note: T. Rex was a 1970s glam rock band, an example of a band
on can mean touching, as in resting on a surface
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A dinosaur is pictured brushing against some small leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: T. Rex is not the dinosaur but Marc Bolan's band; 'leaves' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave someone or something behind for good is to abandon it, so these are synonyms.

clue.text: Academic libertine touring Quebec in flamboyant style

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a graduate

indicators.note: touring means going around, so the libertine surrounds the Quebec letter

parts.note: a roué is a debauched man
Quebec is Q in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A scholarly playboy travels round Quebec in showy fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: Baroque art and architecture is highly ornate and extravagant, hence a flamboyant manner.

clue.text: Nice street contains gym, the bit Sunil mainly uses?

indicators.note: contains says one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: rue is French for street, as spoken in Nice
PE is physical education, gym lessons at school

explanation.surface: A street in Nice has a gym, used mostly by a man named Sunil.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice is the French city, not the adjective; Sunil is a common Indian name, hence the currency.
explanation.definitionFit: The rupee is the money of India, so it is the coin a typical Indian, Sunil, would mostly spend.

clue.text: Snack before tea, reportedly taking the third out of eagerness

parts.note: pre is a prefix meaning before

indicators.note: reportedly means as spoken, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: the drink's name sounds like the letter

indicators.note: the third letter of the eagerness word is removed

parts.note: zeal is keenness or eagerness

explanation.surface: Someone eagerly grabs a snack before tea time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly' turns 'tea' into T; 'taking the third out of' drops A from ZEAL to leave ZEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A pretzel is a knotted baked bread snack, crisp or soft.

clue.text: Ridicule her rear wheels

parts.note: ships are referred to as her, and a ship's poop is its stern deck
wheels are round, so two O shapes

explanation.surface: Mocking the back wheels on a woman's car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'her' is a ship, as ships are called she; its rear is the poop deck.
explanation.definitionFit: To poo-poo an idea is to dismiss it scornfully, which is to ridicule it.

clue.text: Swimmer's Afro half-cut roughly

indicators.note: half-cut is British slang for drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: the suffix ish means approximately or roughly

explanation.surface: A swimmer's Afro hairstyle has been given a rough half-trim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-cut' looks like a haircut but means drunk, shuffling AFRO into OARF.
explanation.definitionFit: The oarfish is a very long, ribbon-like deep-sea fish, so it swims.

clue.text: Model regularly fiddles with nails, losing odd bits

indicators.note: regularly means taking letters at regular intervals, here every second one
dropping the odd-numbered letters of both words leaves only the even-placed ones

explanation.surface: A fashion model keeps fiddling with chipped nails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like the person in the scene but is the definition, a perfect example.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal is a perfect example to follow, a paragon or model.

clue.text: They test beer with disguises, one conceded

parts.note: ale is a type of beer

indicators.note: something conceded is given up, so the letter for one is surrendered

parts.note: veils hide the face, and so disguise
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Drinkers test some beer while in disguise, and one of them gives in.
explanation.walkthrough: A levels are the British school exams taken at about 18; 'conceded' removes I from VEILS.
explanation.definitionFit: A levels are examinations, so they are what test British pupils before university.

clue.text: Needle and threads

definitions.meaning: to needle someone is to irritate or annoy them; as a noun, a fit of irritation
threads is slang for clothes, and this stiff ribbed cotton is a fabric used for them

explanation.definitionFit: Irritation or resentment is one sense; the other is a ribbed cotton material, so cloth for clothing.

clue.text: Male, one that's dropped off vehicle

parts.note: a bull is the male of cattle and other animals
a dozer is someone who dozes, having dropped off to sleep

explanation.surface: A man, one who has fallen asleep, got off a vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropped off' suggests getting off a vehicle but means falling asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A bulldozer is a heavy tracked vehicle with a front blade for clearing earth.

clue.text: Tax excessively? That's right for a supremo

indicators.note: for means one thing replacing another, so right stands in the place of a

parts.note: to overload is to tax or burden too heavily

explanation.surface: Is taxing too heavily the right policy for a leader?
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's right for a' swaps the A in OVERLOAD for R.
explanation.definitionFit: An overlord is a ruler with supreme power over others, which is what a supremo is.

clue.text: Grating good cheese from France (not Belgium), around two pounds

indicators.note: around says the shortened cheese surrounds the pounds
not says the Belgium letter is excluded

parts.note: brie is a soft French cheese
B is the international vehicle code for Belgium
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra, so two of them make LL

explanation.surface: A good French cheese, not one from Belgium, costs about two pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: B for Belgium is the international car code; L for pound comes from the Latin libra.
explanation.definitionFit: A grille is a grating or lattice of bars, as across a window or car front.
